P769
Plasmapheresis in treatment of stiff-man syndrome with a negative
anti-GAD antibody
J. Svatova, H. Machova, J. Pitha (Prague, Czech Republic)
We report the effects of double ﬁltration plasma exchange, which were
performed for a case of stiff-man syndrome even though the patient was
negative for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibody.
Stiff-man syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by progressive
rigidity, stiffness and painful spasms of axial and extremity muscles. The
etiology of SMS is unknown but evidence suggests a possible autoimmune
basis. An autoimmune pathogenesis is suspected because of the presence of
antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme
for the synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric
acid, the association of the disease with other autoimmune conditions, the
presence of various autoantibodies and a strong immunogenetic
association.
We describe a female patient, aged 48 years, suffering from stiff-man
syndrome diagnosed by clinical criteria and electromyography. She had an
8-years history of progressive painful stiffness of her back and limbs,
muscle cramps and dif ﬁculty in walking. Abdominal and paraspinal mus-
cles and limbs were continuously contracting con ﬁrmed by surface and
needle electromyography. Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
and pancraetic islet cells in the serum and cerebrospinal ﬂuid were nega-
tive. She had been taking oral olprazolam and thiocolchicosid. The patient
underwent a course of 6 doubleﬁltration plasma exchange of 2,500 ml each
in a 2-day period. Plasmaspheresis resulted in marked clinical improve-
ment, which continued over 5 months after the plasma exchange.
Plasmapheresis is one choice in the management for the stiff-man
syndrome and favorable response to plasmapheresis has been reported.
